theme: He drew me out of the pit, waiting and the new song
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 40:1-10. The psalm moves from a testimony of patient waiting to a new song and then to a public declaration. Read it as the testimony of someone who has been rescued and cannot keep quiet. You will meet this psalm again in the book of Hebrews, where it is heard as the voice of Christ.
settingTheScene: After the despair of Samson and the confession of Psalm 130, this psalm is the answer that follows a long wait. David has been in a pit, and God has lifted him out. This is a psalm of testimony and gratitude. Its opening verses are some of the best-loved in the Psalter. In this unit, we read it as a response to the story of Judges: when God’s people cry out, he answers, and a new song follows. In the weeks ahead you will encounter it again in Hebrews, and see how its deeper meaning points to Christ.
observation: “I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry” (v. 1).
“He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure” (v. 2).
“He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God” (v. 3).
“Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD” (v. 3).
“Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust” (v. 4).
“Many, O LORD my God, are the wonders you have done, and your thoughts toward us” (v. 5).
“Sacrifice and offering you have not desired, but you have given me an open ear” (v. 6).
“I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with the experience of waiting. “I waited patiently.” In Hebrew the phrase is intensive: “waiting, I waited.” It was a long season. The person who wrote this did not receive an instant answer. We often want God to rescue us quickly, and he may not. But the psalm says that in the waiting, he “inclined” to David and heard. The image is of someone bending down to hear a faint voice. God stoops to listen.

The pit is a vivid image of helplessness. The “miry bog” is a place where every effort to escape makes you sink deeper. David was unable to rescue himself. God lifted him out and set his feet on a rock. The contrast is physical: from sinking mud to solid stone. And then “making my steps secure.” The rescue is not only an escape but a new stability.

The new song is the natural response. God puts it in David’s mouth. The song is not a performance but a gift. And it has a purpose: “Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD.” David’s testimony is meant to draw others in. A rescued person is a living witness.

Verses 6-8 are the center of the psalm. David says that sacrifice and offering were not the thing God ultimately desired. What he wanted was a hearing heart, an “open ear,” and a life of obedience from within. “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.” David’s gratitude is not expressed in religious activity but in wholehearted obedience. This does not abolish sacrifice. It places it in its proper context. Outward rituals without inward devotion are empty.

The last verses commit David to public testimony. He has not hidden God’s righteousness in his heart. He has told the great congregation about God’s faithfulness and salvation. A person rescued from a pit has something to say. In the book of Hebrews, the middle verses are heard in the voice of Christ, who came into the world to do the Father’s will. You will read that when you reach Hebrews 10. For now, rejoice that God hears, lifts, and gives a new song.
connection: The pit imagery recalls Joseph in Genesis 37, and Jeremiah 38 and Jonah 2. The new song appears in Psalms 33:3, 96:1, 98:1, and Revelation 5:9. The priority of obedience over sacrifice is in 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalm 51:16-17, and Hosea 6:6. Hebrews 10:5-10 quotes verses 6-8 as the words of Christ. Romans 10:9-10 links heart faith with public confession.
application:
If you are in a season of waiting, take heart. Read verse 1 slowly. God bends down to hear. Bring a specific request to him today, and commit to waiting on him without a deadline.

If God has rescued you from something, write out your “new song.” It might be a paragraph describing what he did. Share it with someone this week.

Finally, ask yourself where your obedience has become outward only. Pray verse 8, “I delight to do your will,” and ask the Spirit to write God’s law within your heart.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for drawing you out of a pit, and name one.
Ask him to teach you to wait patiently and delight in his will.
Ask him to give you a new song and someone to tell of it.
